a_telling: I moved out on March 1, and Evan kept $1,200 of my $1,500 deposit for cleaning and carpet replacement. Sure, I left three large wine stains on the carpet and scuff marks on the walls—I admit that. But here’s the thing: Evan had promised in February to replace that aging carpet before my lease ended, and he never did. So why should I pay for a carpet he already planned to pitch? He hired a professional cleaning service for $400, and the lease did say I had to return the place broom-clean and damage-free, but I gave him my new mailing address on March 2, right after moving out. He ignored that and mailed the itemized deduction list to the old apartment address on April 15—12 days after the legal deadline. That’s not my fault. Also, I declined his request for a pre-move-out walkthrough—maybe that was a mistake, but he had plenty of chances to inspect. And yes, I made a late rent payment in September, and he sent a written warning about it, but that’s a separate issue, not a reason to steal my deposit. He never proved the carpet needed full replacement, and his timing and address were wrong. I want the whole $1,500 back.
b_telling: I withheld $1,200 of Maya’s $1,500 deposit because she left the apartment in bad shape. She moved out on March 1, and the carpet had three large wine stains and the walls had scuff marks—that’s damage, not normal wear. The lease clearly required her to return it broom-clean and damage-free, and she didn’t. I had to hire a professional cleaning service for $400 to make it habitable, and the carpet needed replacement. Look, I know I promised in February to replace the aging carpet before her lease ended, but I never got around to it, and that’s on me—but her stains made it worse, and she still caused damage. She declined my request for a pre-move-out walkthrough, so I couldn’t assess things with her. She did give me her new mailing address on March 2, but I accidentally sent the itemized list to the old apartment on April 15—I admit that was 12 days after the legal deadline, but I was busy dealing with the mess she left. Also, she made a late rent payment in September and got a written warning; that shows she wasn’t always responsible. The deductions are justified, and I’m keeping the $1,200.

a_telling: I emailed David on June 1 about the leaking sink and warped cabinet. He said he'd send a plumber next week, but by June 10 nothing. I emailed again. He said plumber was scheduled for June 15. That plumber came, but said the part wasn't in stock and he'd order it. I waited. On June 20 I texted that I expected action that week. Then on June 22, David finally ordered the part himself after learning the plumber hadn't ordered it. Meanwhile, I was so fed up that on June 25 I sent a formal complaint to the property management company, without telling David first. The part arrived June 28 and the plumber fixed it on July 1. But then on July 2, David sent me an invoice for $50 for 'extra communication handling.' That's ridiculous – I only communicated because he didn't handle things. I want him to waive the fee and apologize for the delay. I admit I went over his head, but I was desperate.
b_telling: I got Maya's email on June 1 about the sink. I replied on June 3 that I'd send a plumber next week. No plumber came, so she emailed again on June 10. I responded on June 11 that it was scheduled for June 15. The plumber came and said the part wasn't in stock and he'd order it. Then Maya texted me on June 20, being rude. I assumed the plumber had ordered it, but on June 22 I found out he hadn't, so I ordered it online myself. Meanwhile, on June 25, Maya sent a formal complaint to the property management company without even telling me – that was an unfair move, going behind my back. The part arrived June 28 and the plumber fixed it on July 1. Then I sent her an invoice for $50 for 'extra communication handling' because she made so many unnecessary contacts. She should pay that and acknowledge that her complaint to management was unfair. I did my best despite the plumber's mistake.

a_telling: On January 1, 2025, I signed a 12-month lease with Lisa for my apartment 4B, starting February 1, with monthly rent of $1200. The lease explicitly stated that early termination requires 60 days' notice and a $2000 lease-break fee. On June 15, she gave me written notice that she'd move out on July 1. She actually moved out on July 5, and she didn't pay rent for August. I inspected the unit—it was undamaged, just slightly dusty. I listed it on August 1 and found a new tenant who moved in on September 1. I sent her a bill for the $2000 fee on August 10. She said she lost her job and had to move to a cheaper city, and she offered $500 as a 'goodwill' fee. I refused and demanded the full $2000 per the lease. I feel that she signed a contract and my costs are real—even though I found a new tenant quickly, the fee is for the inconvenience and the lease's terms. She put me in a bind by leaving early, and I'm just enforcing what we both agreed to. I think it's fair to hold her to it.
b_telling: I'm Lisa. I rented apartment 4B from Mark under a one-year lease starting February 1, 2025, at $1200 per month. The lease had an early termination clause: 60 days' notice and a $2000 fee. On June 15, I wrote to Mark that I'd move out July 1. I actually left on July 5. I didn't pay rent for August because I was already out. Mark inspected and said the place was undamaged, just dusty. He listed it on August 1 and got a new tenant for September 1. He sent me a bill for the full $2000 on August 10. I told him I lost my job and had to move to a cheaper city. I offered $500 as a goodwill gesture. He refused and demands the full $2000. I think that's harsh because he didn't lose any rent—he had a new tenant by September, and the apartment was fine. I'm struggling financially, and $2000 would break me. I'm not trying to weasel out, but I gave notice and he found someone quickly. I hope he understands my situation.
